old: he used to say in his quaint way:
new: he used to say in his quaint way (Cain being the man in Genesis who asked, “Am I my brother’s keeper?”):
reason: Source “I incline to Cain’s heresy” is a biblical allusion a listener may not catch; brief accurate gloss of Genesis 4:9 without interpretation.

old: so ugly that it brought out a cold sweat
new: so ugly that it brought the sweat out on me as if I’d been running
reason: Source “brought out the sweat on me like running”: candidate drops the running simile and adds “cold”.

new: the usual cut-and-dry apothecary—the ordinary kind of doctor of the day—
reason: Source calls the doctor an “apothecary”; modern listeners hear “pharmacist” and may think a different person is meant; brief gloss (Victorian apothecaries were general practitioners).

old: the more it looks like Queer Street, the less I ask.
new: the more it looks like Queer Street—like trouble, or something shady—the less I ask.
reason: Source “Queer Street” is Victorian slang for trouble or disreputable/financially shaky affairs; opaque (and misleading) to a modern listener without a brief gloss.

new: The will was holographic—written entirely in Jekyll’s own hand—because
reason: Source “The will was holograph” is a legal term the following clause depends on (Utterson refused to help write it); brief gloss.

old: as a man who loved the sane and conventional sides of life, to whom the fanciful was the immodest.
new: as a man who loved the sane and conventional sides of life, and who found anything fanciful immodest.
reason: Source “to whom the fanciful was the immodest” kept verbatim is hard to parse aloud; same meaning in plain order.

old: would have estranged Damon and Pythias.”
new: would have estranged Damon and Pythias—the most devoted friends in legend.”
reason: Source “would have estranged Damon and Pythias” depends on knowing they are the proverbial ideal friends of Greek legend; brief gloss.

new: (except in the matter of conveyancing—the legal work of transferring property)
reason: Source “conveyancing” is a legal term the joke turns on; brief gloss.

old: the face of a man without bowels of mercy—
new: the face of a man without bowels of mercy—a man without pity—
reason: Source “without bowels of mercy” is a biblical idiom (bowels = seat of compassion) that a listener will likely misread; brief gloss keeps the phrase.

old: a strong, almost superstitious foresight of success
new: a strong, superstitious foresight of success
reason: Source “a strong, superstitious prevision of success” has no hedge; “almost” softens the certainty.

old: turned with an air of defiance
new: turned to face him with an air of defiance
reason: Source “fronted about” means turned to face him—the point, since Hyde had avoided looking at him and Utterson asked to see his face; “turned” alone loses that.

new: Something troglodytic—like a cave-dweller—shall we say?
reason: Source “troglodytic” is a rare word central to the image; brief gloss (troglodyte = cave-dweller).

old: Or can it be the old story of Dr. Fell?
new: Or can it be the old story of Dr. Fell—disliking a man without being able to say why?
reason: Source “the old story of Dr. Fell” alludes to the rhyme “I do not love thee, Dr. Fell … the reason why I cannot tell”; without a gloss the allusion is lost; gloss states only the rhyme's content.

old: “I have a feeling he is in deep water!
new: “I fear he is in deep water!
reason: Source “my mind misgives me he is in deep waters” expresses foreboding; “I have a feeling” is neutral.

old: punishment coming, pede claudo, years after
new: punishment coming, pede claudo—on limping foot—years after
reason: Source Latin “pede claudo” (Horace: punishment follows with limping foot) is untranslated; a listener cannot follow it; literal gloss only.
